title: Revealing Networks: Understanding Effective Teacher Practices in AI-Supported Classrooms using Transmodal Ordered Network Analysis
venue: The 14th Learning Analytics and Knowledge Conference (LAK '24)
extended_summary:
This paper asks whether adding classroom context data to student tutor log data improves understanding of learning in AI-supported classrooms, and what teacher practices are associated with better or worse student progress. The authors focus on teacher-student interactions around the use of an AI tutor, especially teacher monitoring, talking to students, and brief visits, to explain differences in students’ learning rates within the system.

The study uses a multimodal case study from a middle school math classroom using the Lynnette AI tutor for linear equation solving. Data came from 85 seventh-grade students across five classes taught by one experienced teacher in a U.S. public school over three class sessions. The researchers combined tutor log data, classroom observation codes, and teacher position-sensor data, then analyzed them with transmodal ordered network analysis (T/ONA) and qualitative text replay of observation notes. Students were grouped by low vs. high learning rates, and also by whether they had been visited by the teacher.

The main finding is that teacher-practice data improved prediction of student learning rates beyond tutor logs alone. Teacher screen alignment and teacher talking were especially informative: low-learning-rate students tended to request hints after these teacher actions, while high-learning-rate students more often produced correct attempts. After teacher visits, low-learning-rate students’ behavior shifted toward more consecutive correct attempts, suggesting visits were associated with more favorable learning patterns. Qualitative notes suggest that low-learning-rate students often received more procedural help before visits, while visits were more likely to include conceptual support and self-explanation prompts. The authors conclude that making teacher practices visible through analytics could inform dashboards and reflection tools for improving AI-supported classroom instruction.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed observational classroom study using multimodal learning analytics and quantitative ethnography, not an RCT. It provides careful triangulation of log data, observation notes, and teacher positioning, but causal claims remain limited.
impact_tier_rationale: The findings are relevant to AI-supported classroom practice and teacher guidance, but they are mainly correlational/interpretive rather than direct evidence of learning gains from an intervention. Effects are described as improved inference and behavior patterns rather than a clear, generalizable achievement impact of at least modest size.

interventions.use_case: Classroom use of the Lynnette AI tutor for 7th-grade linear equation solving, with step-wise feedback, hints, and mastery-style problem solving practice.

finding.finding_summary: In a 3-day classroom study with 85 seventh-grade students, adding out-of-tutor teacher practice codes to the model improved inference of students’ learning-rate group in the AI tutor. The multimodal model had lower AIC than the in-tutor-only model (AIC=150.60 vs 158.30; t=12.76, 95% CI [7.06, 9.63], p<.001), and students with high learning rates showed more consecutive correct attempts (e.g., FIRST CORRECT ATTEMPT → CORRECT ATTEMPT m_high=0.43 vs m_low=0.29).
finding.measure: AI tutor learning rate / first-attempt correctness, ordered network connections among equation-solving behaviors
finding.confidence_interval: [7.06, 9.63] for AIC difference; other effect sizes reported as rank-based r values

finding.finding_summary: Teacher practices associated with conceptual support were linked to more desirable student problem-solving behavior, especially after teacher visits. After visits, low-learning-rate students showed a much stronger shift toward consecutive correct attempts (FIRST CORRECT ATTEMPT → CORRECT ATTEMPT from m_pre=0.14 to m_post=0.50, V=16, r=0.92, p<.001), suggesting improved strategic use of the tutor and more effective problem solving.
finding.measure: Ordered network transitions among tutor behaviors before vs. after teacher visits
finding.study_size: n=85 students; visit analyses conducted within student groups

finding.finding_summary: The study suggests that teacher monitoring and talking were often followed by hint requests among low-learning-rate students, a pattern the authors interpret as potentially reflecting disengagement or reliance on procedural help. In contrast, teacher visits and more conceptual support were associated with improved in-tutor behavior afterward, including more correct attempts, indicating a mixed relationship between classroom support, engagement, and learning behavior.
finding.measure: Hint requests, detector-coded struggling/idling/tutor misuse, and post-visit behavior patterns
finding.effect_size: multiple rank-based r values; strongest reported r=0.61 and r=0.92
